sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Le Sueur County
sections.html:
Value and class come from the Assessor. The tax itself is figured and collected by the Auditor-Treasurer. The Assessor's office is at 88 S Park Avenue, Le Center, MN 56057, phone 507-357-8213.

The staff covers about 19,000 parcels in 14 townships and 10 cities. Their work is estimating market value, sorting property by its main use (residential, agricultural, seasonal or commercial) and ruling on which parcels get homestead. Each year a sales study compares assessed values to real sales, and the Minnesota Department of Revenue expects the estimate to land between 90% and 105% of actual market value.

On the billing side, each taxing district certifies its levy, and the Auditor-Treasurer converts those levies into a bill using the Assessor's values and the state's classifications. The same office processes real estate transactions for property in the county.

Along the Minnesota River in south central Minnesota, Le Sueur County is counted in the Minneapolis-St. Paul-Bloomington metro area. It had 29,453 residents in July 2025, a 2.8% gain on the 28,663 of 2020. There are 13,256 housing units, and 81.0% of occupied homes are owner occupied. The median owner-occupied home is worth $316,500, and median household income is $94,968.

The county is largely rural, with 85.8% of residents outside urban areas in 2020. Cities include Le Center (the seat), Le Sueur, Montgomery, Waterville, Elysian, New Prague, Cleveland, Kasota, Kilkenny and Heidelberg. Agricultural, seasonal and residential are separate classes, so a lake or farm parcel can be taxed differently from a house in town, and the Assessor sets the class on acreage and farmland by how it is used.

Accepted payment types are cash, check, money order, card and ACH. A third-party processor runs card payments and adds a 2.5% convenience fee.

The county's Beacon mapping application lets you look up a property, view a map and pay taxes online. Beacon also has subscription services for name searches and comparable property searches. A single-family property tax calculator spreadsheet, certified tax rates for 2025 and 2026, and levy history sit on the Property Tax Info page, so you can see how much of a bill comes from each taxing district before you list.

The due dates printed on your statement are the ones that count, and the state rule is summarized in the next section.

State law divides a bill over $100 into a spring half, due before May 16, and a fall half, due before October 16. A bill of $100 or less is paid whole at the spring date.

How the penalty grows (Minnesota Statutes 279.01)
StepHomesteadNonhomestead
Not paid by the due date2%4%
Still open on the 1st of next monthAdditional 2%Additional 4%
Every month after, to December1% more1% more
Cap8%12%

A statement mailed after April 24 pushes the first-half deadline to 21 days after its postmark, and penalties run from that later date.

Every March the Assessor sends each owner a valuation notice that names the local Board of Appeal and Equalization, the place to object. Meeting dates are posted on the county's schedule page, and your notice gives the time and location.

Going to court means following section 278.01 of Minnesota Statutes: serve a petition on the county auditor and file it with the district court administrator by April 30 of the payable year. Tax Court is the alternative, and its appeal opens when the notice lands and closes the day before May 1. Before filing, check with the Auditor-Treasurer on whether you must make a minimum payment.

sections.h2: Reading your statement and the county's tools
sections.html:
Start with the parcel number, since every lookup in the county's systems runs through it. The statement shows what each taxing district asked for, and the certified tax rates for 2025 and 2026 posted on the Property Tax Info page let you check those figures against the county's own list. The levy history on the same page shows how each district's request has moved, which helps explain why a bill went up even when your value did not.

If you want to see how a comparable house is treated, Beacon's property search lets you look at neighboring parcels and their maps. Pairing that with the assessor's yearly sales study is a reasonable way to judge whether your value is in line before the March notice arrives. The Department of Revenue expects assessed values to sit between 90% and 105% of actual market value, so a number far outside that range is worth a call to 507-357-8213.

Homeowners whose tax is high compared with household income may get a state property tax refund, the first item on the county's Property Tax Info page. Claims are due August 15 with the Department of Revenue, and late ones are taken for a year.

The Assessor decides which parcels qualify for homestead classification, and as the penalty table shows, homestead owners start at a lower rate. If you have moved out or the house is empty after an estate, ask the Assessor whether the homestead status ends and when.

sections.h2: What closing looks like on the tax side
sections.html:
On closing day the tax work comes down to three numbers: what you owe for the current year through the day you hand over the keys, any special assessment balance, and any penalty on an old installment. Your title company will ask the county for these. Giving the Auditor-Treasurer your parcel number and expected closing date ahead of time lets them quote an exact payoff instead of an estimate.

When both halves of the year are already paid, there is little left to do except agree with the buyer on how the year is divided. When a half is open, the payoff comes out of your proceeds at the table. Either way, the buyer has to apply for homestead on their own if they plan to live in the house, since the seller's status does not transfer by itself.

sections.h2: Checklist before selling a Le Sueur County house
sections.html:
Confirm both halves of the current year are paid, get the parcel's special assessment balance, and compare the next due date with your closing date. The Auditor-Treasurer's office handles real estate transactions, so a stop there before closing keeps surprises off the settlement statement.

Bring the parcel number, your latest statement and the date you hope to close, and let the office give you the amount to pay through that date. Ask the Assessor to confirm the parcel's class too. A lake lot or acreage can sit in a different class than the house beside it, and a buyer's lender may ask about it.

If the property is inherited or has been empty, add one more question: whether any older year is open. Settle that first, because a payoff that leaves an earlier year out will surface again at the title company, and a cash sale does not remove the need to clear it.

faqs.q: What is the Le Sueur County Assessor's address?
faqs.a: 88 S Park Avenue, Le Center, MN 56057, phone 507-357-8213. Le Center is also the county seat.

faqs.q: Does Le Sueur County charge a fee for card payments?
faqs.a: Yes. A 2.5% convenience fee is added when a credit or debit card is run. Cash, check, money order and ACH are also accepted.

faqs.q: When does the Le Sueur County board of appeal meet?
faqs.a: It meets once a year, with the date and time printed on your March valuation notice and posted on the county's schedule page. Notices for the next year go out each March.

faqs.q: How many parcels does Le Sueur County have?
faqs.a: Nearly 19,000, spread across 14 townships and 10 cities.

faqs.q: Can I file for the state property tax refund after August 15?
faqs.a: Yes, for up to one year after the due date, which is August 15.
